explanation: No clear shared feature. Top examples include the space before a year after 'from/to/in' (e.g. 'from 1727 to[ ]1747'), but also code tokens (' char', ' static', ' c'), HTML 'lang', and assorted prose words (' good', ' such', ' of', ' greatly'). The year-space case is the most repeated pattern, but many unrelated tokens fire about as strongly.

Mostly the future/auxiliary verb ' will' (and contractions like 'I'll' / 'I've') after a subject or relative 'that', e.g. 'a measure that[ will]', 'he[ will]'. It also fires on unrelated things such as the mojibake 'xe2x8[0]' sequence, ' public' in Java, and '$.'. Mid and weak activations are scattered.

Mixed. Recurring pieces are 'path[ogenic]' (in pathogenic/nonpathogenic), ' the' after 'save/saved' ('Save the dates', 'saved the life', 'God Save the Queen'), 'Democratic Republic[ of]', 'slowed/slower', and digits inside RFC/ISO numbers. No single concept ties these together.

French-language text: fires on function words and word starts in French prose and in French code comments (' qui', ' a', ' le', ' l', 'Quelqu'un', the '#' before a French shell comment). It is weaker on other Romance/foreign text, on '<' opening XML tags, and on ' United' in 'United States/Nations'.

A comma or ' in' at a clause boundary in formal legal or patent prose: 'are already known[,] but', 'relates,[ in] general', 'and[,] more particularly', 'affirm[ in] all other respects'. It is moderate on similar commas or ' in' in scientific abstracts and weak elsewhere.

Early in a sentence, the token right after an introductory phrase or clause: ''s' in 'In this week's / In today's', ' of' in 'In the theory of / For assessment of', and the subject ' it/we/the/a' after an opening adverbial clause plus comma ('When doped with boron,[ it]'). Weak on ordinary commas.

A content word or modifier just after a determiner or degree word in evaluative or descriptive phrasing: emphatic ' even' ('didn't even', 'never even'), and nouns or adjectives after 'a common/the/an' ('common[ cause]', 'the[ prototype]', 'an[ important]', 'two[ typical]'). Broad and somewhat diffuse.

Mixed. It fires on many non-English tokens (Czech ' se', Dutch ' paar', Danish ' at', Norwegian ' det', German 'unk', Chinese), on URL/path fragments ('/w', '/C'), on ' case' in a switch, and on English function words (' the', ' not', ' really', ' also'). No coherent single trigger.

Mixed. Strongest consistent pattern is ' the' in license boilerplate 'See[ the] License/LICENSE file', but it also fires on word-internal subword pieces in medical, Dutch and German words ('oil[seed]', 'conserv[ing]', 'Epile[psy]', 'Parapleg[ic]', 'vorge[gang]en') and on abbreviation pieces like 'N[.J]' and ' Cal'.

The first subword piece of a word split into several tokens, especially ' st' at the start of words ('st'enosis, 'st'ents, 'st'unts, 'st'ability, 'st'ably), plus other word-initial fragments (' impr', ' conf', ' ent', 'Sup', ' sup', 'F[IF]'). A whole common word does not fire.

Tokens inside programming Q&A or code-comment text, especially a noun or determiner naming the technical object being discussed ('from a[ nib]', 'your[ AJAX] call', 'with[ this] regexp', 'a[ jQuery] scroll event', 'a cookie with[ a] key'). It also fires on identifiers in code. Ordinary non-technical prose is weak.

Subword pieces in the middle of rare or foreign words and names: Polish, Slovenian, Czech, Hungarian, Dutch and Norwegian words, place names, drug and taxon names ('Lam[iv]udine', 'herpes[v]irus', 'Nau[v]oo', 'B[ost]an', ' G'mina'), plus a few code/URL fragments. It is weak on common English words.

Mixed. It fires on ' =' in JS/Swift variable assignments ('var params[ =]'), on contractions after 'we' ('We'll', 'we're'), on 'How[ long]', and on internal subword pieces of words ('kind[erg]arteners', 'par[ishes]', 'Phil[har]monic', 'ear[w]ax'). These do not share one theme.

A modal or verb right after a subject in a 'when/how/to' clause, especially after 'I' or 'can' ('when I[ can]', 'how I[ can]', 'how you[ want]', 'can[ only]', 'will[ need]', 'To[ better]'). A few prepositions after people/groups also fire ('civilians[ in]', 'people[ in]').

The ' case' keyword at the start of a switch-statement branch is the strongest trigger. Secondary activations land on class or type names in code (' Component', ' Context', ' TestCase', ' setContentView') and on subword pieces inside foreign personal names ('Talak[uli]', 'Benbi[hi]', 'Zac[colo]').

End-of-line tokens in code and markup: the token that ends a line together with the newline (';⏎', '}⏎', '>⏎', ')⏎', '"⏎', ',⏎'), when it is followed by indentation in deeply nested code, XML or JSON. Strongest inside indented blocks.

The opening parenthesis plus variable of a function definition in math word problems, like 'Let b[(n]) =' or 'Let t[(g]) ='. It is weaker on similar variable or parameter binding in code (lambda/LINQ 'from x', 'function(v', 'for (int i', 'except Exception as').

Tokens in non-English text, especially Slavic (Czech, Russian), German, Scandinavian and Vietnamese: sentence-initial words or function words like Russian 'Как', 'люб-', German ' so', Danish 'Jeg', Czech ' v'. It is weaker on subword pieces of foreign names, and English text barely fires.

A word-internal subword piece right after a hyphen, dot or other split inside a compound or identifier, often an 'h' piece ('pull[-h]itter', 'NTLM[-h]ashed', 'hard[-h]itting', 'button[-h]ref', 'vingt[-h]uit'). It also fires on fragments like '.p12', '.n', and Hungarian/German word pieces.

The first subword piece of a word, often a prefix, split across tokens, mostly in French, Italian, Greek or Dutch text and in rare English words ('dis[ench]anted', ' ass'urer, ' rec'upero, ' ré'duit, ' fl'imsiness, ' AP'PEALS, ' Ab'strium). It is weak on whole common words.

No clear unifying feature. Triggers include the digits in timestamps ('Updated: ... 1[4]:36 IST'), sentence-final periods in headline-like or encyclopedic text, ''s' in 'Elin's', ' recently', 'by way of[ example]', and 'without[ replacement]'. These look like several unrelated jobs.
